steps.title: Tell Us About the Tree
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to send first: what the tree is if they know, roughly how tall it stands against the house, what they have noticed and where it stands (near the house, the road, next door, an overhead line), photos taken from the ground if they have them. Never ask the customer to climb, get a ladder out or go near a hanging branch. No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Come and Look at the Tree

steps.title: We Do the Work on a Date That Suits You

Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan (step 2 and Why choose us own them). Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it). A nest found on the day can move that part of the work to later: say so only as what usually applies, with no date.

steps_emergency.title: Call Us

faq_slots.question: Does my tree need to come down, or can it be pruned?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Felling is not the default. Say when removal is right: a tree that is dead, decayed through, structurally failed, or standing where its size can never fit (Table A and B tree removal). Then that most worries are answered by a reduction back to growth points, a lift of the lower crown, dead wood taken out, or support for a weak fork (Table A pruning and cabling: support, not a cure). What decides it: what the tree is, what is wrong with it, what stands under it, and what is found when it is looked at. Never that a tree is safe or unsafe, never a percentage of crown, never topping as an option.

faq_slots.question: Why is my tree dropping branches or going thin at the top?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Say first when it is normal: some trees shed small dead wood every year and most drop leaves early in a dry summer. Then three genuinely different causes in plain words: dead wood the tree has given up on, disease showing in the crown (ash dieback where the research supports it locally: blackened leaves, bare patches, dark marks on the bark, Table B and E), and damage at the roots from digging, compacted ground or a change in the water around them. Then what the local ground adds, then what a look at the tree decides. Never that the tree is dying.

faq_slots.question: Should a stump be ground out or left to rot?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What decides it: what the ground is wanted for afterwards (Table A and E stump removal: the finish and the depth are agreed to the intended use, deeper for planting than for grass, with no measurement given). Leaving it: slow to break down, and some species send up shoots from live roots (Table B and E). Grinding: the stump and the main root plate ground out, the chippings cleared or left as agreed, the hole backfilled, the larger roots staying in the ground to rot in their own time (no number of years: the facts give none). Never say grinding stops every shoot.

faq_slots.question: What time of year is best for tree work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing cells, with the reason in the tree or in what usually applies: felling, dismantling, stump grinding and making safe run through the year subject to wildlife, ground and safe weather; pruning generally after the leaves have hardened in late spring and summer, with species differences (some bleed sap if cut as growth starts, so they are cut in summer or midwinter; a few are summer only); planting and moving a tree while it is dormant, from autumn to early spring; a deciduous hedge renovated in midwinter and an evergreen one in mid spring. A nest being built or used stops that part of the work until it is empty, and there is no blanket ban on the season. No dates, nothing about a busy time of year.

faq_slots.question: Will I need permission before work on my tree?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with 'usually' or 'in most cases'. A tree with an order on it: the council's consent comes first, and the business makes that application for the customer only where [CV: handles_planning] says so. A tree in a conservation area: the council is told ahead of the work, the number of weeks only as the rule row gives it. A dead tree or an immediate danger has a narrower route of its own (notice, or only the necessary work and the council told after). A garden tree usually needs no felling licence. Nests and roosts stay protected whether or not the tree is. No figure, no diameter, never an Act's or an order's name.

cards.title: A tree that's outgrown its place
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: a tree that now shades the whole garden, branches at the gutters or across the roof, a hedge wider than the path it stands beside, a crown blocking the light to a room. The one cause this card makes: growth the garden has run out of room for. What decides it: what the tree is and how it responds to a cut (Table A pruning: a reduction specified by its size back to suitable side branches, a lift of the lower crown for clearance, a thinning that keeps the outline; Table E: never topping, which leaves a mass of shoots and open wounds). What the work gives them, in plain words: light back in the garden, clearance from the house, a hedge brought back to a width in stages at its season. Never a lifestyle pitch, never a fault invented for it, never a percentage of crown.
cards.mechanism: growth the garden has run out of room for

cards.title: A split, a crack or a lean that wasn't there before
cards.brief: Problem led: a trunk that has split, a fork that has opened, a limb that has torn, a lean that has appeared or grown since the last storm, cracked or lifted soil at the base (Table B tree removal and cabling signs). The one cause this card makes: a fork or a lean that has started to move. Put the cause in the tree: a tight fork with bark grown into the join, old decay where a branch was torn off, roots cut or waterlogged. The honest answer: what it needs depends on what the tree is, how much solid wood remains, and what stands under it; the choices are support for a weak fork (Table A cabling: support, never a repair of decayed wood), a reduction that takes the load off, or removal in sections where the tree cannot be kept (Table A removal). Never that a tree is or is not safe, never felling as the default, never a scare.
cards.mechanism: a fork or a lean that has started to move

cards.title: Fungus at the base, dead wood in the crown, leaves going early
cards.brief: Problem led: brackets or toadstools at the foot of the trunk, dead branches high in the crown, a top going thin, leaves blackening and wilting in summer, dark marks on the bark (Table B and E ash dieback signs; Table B surveys). The one cause this card makes: decay or disease working where it can't be seen. Say first what is normal: a dry summer drops leaves early, and some trees shed small dead wood every year. Then what is not: dieback spreading year on year, a crown thinning from the top, fungus feeding inside the root plate or at the base of the trunk. What decides it is a proper look (Table A surveys: inspect, record, assess), and not every diseased tree comes down (Table E: not every infected ash must be felled; some are kept and watched). Never name a disease the research does not support for the area; never that the tree is dying.
cards.mechanism: decay or disease working where it can't be seen

cards.title: Roots under the paving, the drains or the house
cards.brief: A situation and a warning sign in one: paving lifting beside a tree, roots showing through the lawn, a new surface planned close to a trunk, cracks in a wall near a large tree where the ground is clay (Table B root barriers and surveys; Table E subsidence). The one cause this card makes: roots spreading further than the space left for them. On clay, say what usually applies: the ground gives up its moisture to a big tree through a dry summer and takes it back in winter, so a worry about cracks is investigated before anything is cut, because felling can bring movement of its own (Table E). The options in plain words: a root barrier to steer roots away from what is being built, a reduction to cut the water the tree draws, a survey first where a house is involved (Table A root barriers and surveys). Never promise the cracks stop, never that a tree caused them, never that removal is the answer.
cards.mechanism: roots spreading further than the space left for them

problem_card.title: What a winter gale leaves in the tree
problem_card.brief: Planned work after a storm, never a call out (the emergency variant owns those): say first what is normal after a gale, small dead wood and twigs on the lawn, a few leaves and seed down early. Then what is not: a limb torn and still hanging, a fresh split at a fork, a lean that was not there before the wind, soil lifted on one side of the base (Table B removal and cabling signs). The one cause this card makes: wind finding the dead and weak wood first. What the customer does: keep clear of anything hanging and of the area under it, photograph it from the ground, and never go near it with a ladder or a saw. What usually happens: the tree looked at from the ground, the damage brought down under control, the wound it leaves assessed before any decision about the rest of the tree (Table A pruning and removal). problem_card.mechanism: wind finding the dead and weak wood first

faq_slot.question: Can tree work be done in winter, or while birds are nesting?
faq_slot.answer_brief: What the time of year changes, from the trade facts timing cells and rule rows, with the reason in the tree or in what usually applies: most felling, dismantling and stump work runs through the cold months when the ground and the weather allow; a bare tree is easier to see into and to drop, while the crown's health is easier to judge in leaf (Table A surveys); pruning of many species waits until the leaves have hardened, and the sap bleeders are cut in summer or midwinter; planting and moving happen while the tree is dormant. In spring and summer there is no blanket ban on tree work, but a nest being built or used is left until the young have gone and the work round it waits (Table C and E). Bats roost in old trees and are protected too: a check before the work, written as what usually applies. The nest check as this business's own practice only when nesting_bird_check is confirmed. No dates.

cards.title: A tree down across the drive or the road

What the customer does first: keep people and cars off it and away from the root plate and the crown, never try to cut or drag it, and tell the council or the police where a public road is blocked, as what usually applies. What usually happens when they call: the danger judged from the ground, the area closed off, lines and protections checked, the trunk cut into pieces under control and the way cleared; the stump and the rest of the timber dealt with as planned work (Table A emergency tree work). cards.title: A split branch hanging over the path

The one cause this card makes: a broken branch still caught in the tree, resting on nothing that can be trusted, so it can fall with no warning and no second gust needed. What the customer does first: keep everyone and everything out from under it, including the car, and never put a ladder or a rope anywhere near it (Table B: working beneath unstable timber is where people get hurt). What usually happens: the branch lowered under control from a safe anchor or a platform, then the tear it leaves behind looked at, because a torn stub is where decay starts (Table A and B pruning). Never promise a time, never that the tree is fine once the branch is down.

cards.title: Branches on or near a power line

What the customer does first: stay well back, keep children and pets indoors, touch nothing in contact with the tree, and call the electricity network operator before anyone else, as what usually applies; the tree surgeon cannot start until the operator has made the line safe or confirmed it is dead. Never a distance in metres, never a voltage, never an instruction to move anything themselves.

What is left of the tree, the stump and the timber is dealt with as planned work on another day (Table A: follow up work may be separate). Never promise everything is done on the first visit. Never mention the price.

faq_slots.question: How much is an emergency [TRADE_PERSON] call out in [CITY]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What moves the price, from the cost cards: the time of day and the day of the week, how far the tree is from the base, the access, what making it safe takes, and that the rest of the tree, the stump and the timber are a second visit priced as its own job. A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; the hours the business comes out only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; an arrival time only from [CV: response_time]. The price agreed before work starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice. No figure.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for emergency tree work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with a plausible tree work example that does not suggest carelessness. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after an emergency job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then that making safe is making safe: the planned work that follows is where the tree, the stump and the timber are dealt with properly, under the reasonable care and skill standard, never as a defence. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: Is this an emergency, or can it wait?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What counts as urgent, from the card list and Table B: a tree or a limb down across a road, a drive, a roof or a car; a torn branch still hanging over where people go; anything touching or near an overhead line; a trunk split or a tree leaning freshly after a storm. What usually waits for planned work: a stump, a tree that has simply grown too big, a hedge over the path, dead wood high in a crown over a bed nobody uses, a lean the tree has had for years. Link one service page. Planned work is never dressed up as urgent.

faq_slots.question: What should I do before you arrive?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From a safe distance only: keep people, cars and pets clear of the tree and of anything it could still fall on, stay out of rooms under a tree on the roof, touch nothing in contact with an overhead line and call the network operator about the line first, photograph what can be seen from the ground (Table B and C emergency). Never an instruction to cut, pull, prop or climb. Whether the business deals with the insurer only from the client values.

faq_slots.question: How quickly can you get to me?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only, as given; a same day visit only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes; work in the tree waits until the wind has dropped and the timber can be reached safely, and a line is dealt with by the network operator first (Table A emergency: wind damage, unstable timber and live lines decide whether work can go ahead). Never '24/7' or 'any time' unless [CV: emergency_callouts] gives it in those words.

faq_slots.question: Will you come out while the storm is still going?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What usually happens: the area made safe and the danger judged from the ground as soon as it is safe to be there; while the wind is still up nobody climbs or works under hung up timber, and a live line waits for the network operator (Table A emergency). Any arrival time from [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only; no out of hours promise unless [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: response_time] gives it.

problem_card.title: What to do while you wait for us
problem_card.brief: What the customer can do from a safe distance, in plain words: keep people, cars and pets away from the tree and from anything it could still fall on, including the part that is still standing; shut the gate or the door that leads under it; if the tree is on the house, stay out of the rooms beneath it until it has been looked at; photograph what can be seen from the ground, then call (whether the business deals with an insurer only from the client values). The one cause this card makes: whatever is still under it, because a tree that has half fallen is not finished moving. Never an instruction to cut, pull, prop or climb anything; never a chainsaw as a job for the reader; never a time by which anyone arrives unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slot.question: Will you come out while the storm is still going?
faq_slot.answer_brief: What usually happens: the area made safe and the danger judged from the ground as soon as it is safe to be there; while the wind is still up nobody climbs or works under hung up timber, and a live line waits for the network operator (Table A emergency). Any arrival time from [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only; a same day visit only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes; no out of hours promise unless [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: response_time] gives it.

items.title: Looking at the tree and what's around it
items.brief: The inspection stage from the trade facts: the tree, what is wrong with it, what stands under it and around it (the house, the road, the neighbour's garden, overhead lines, buried services), and how the crew and the chippings get in and out. A part of the job, not a promise about the quote.

items.title: Checking whether the tree is protected, and for nests
items.brief: The checks before the work, from the trade facts stages: whether an order or a conservation area covers the tree, and whether a nest is in use or a roost is likely. Written as what usually applies. Who sends the notice or makes the application only from [CV: handles_planning]. Never an Act's or an order's name.

items.title: Setting up the work area
items.brief: The exclusion area, the escape routes and the rescue arrangements from the trade facts stages: the part of the garden or the road that is kept clear while the work is on, and why. Said as how the job is done, never as homework for the reader.

items.title: Getting into the tree
items.brief: Climbing or a platform, as the trade facts methods cell has it for this service; which one depends on the tree, its condition and what is around it. A named machine only where [CV: materials_methods] gives it.

items.title: The cuts, the sections or the grind
items.brief: The central stage of the job from the trade facts: the reduction cut back to growth points, the lift, the sections taken down from the top, the stump ground out, the cable fitted, the tree planted, named as the trade names it and in the customer's words. Never a percentage, never a depth.

items.title: Lowering and processing what comes down
items.brief: The lowering, cross cutting and chipping stages from the trade facts: pieces lowered by rope where they cannot be dropped, the timber cut up, the brash chipped. What the customer sees happen in the garden.

items.title: Clearing up and what happens to the timber
items.brief: The last stage from the trade facts: the garden cleared, the chippings and logs taken away, left for a use or stacked for the customer as agreed. Logs left for the customer only from the client values.

cards.title: Dead wood, a dropped branch or a crack you can see from the ground
cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the trade facts signs row for this service, in their words: a dead branch over the path, branches on the roof, a trunk that has split, a fork that has opened, leaves blackening in summer, ivy hiding the trunk, paving lifting by the roots. The one cause this card makes: a part of the tree that has stopped holding its own weight, or holding its place. Put the cause in the tree, from the rows. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: specific, never alarming (a dead branch falls; a weak fork fails in wind; a hidden cavity goes unseen). On a schedule led page (hedge trimming, pollarding and coppicing, repeat crown work, surveys on a cycle) the card is what slips and when: shoots spoiling the line of a hedge by midsummer, old pollard heads carrying long heavy growth, a cycle missed so the next cut goes into bigger wood, with the reason in the tree from the timing cell, never in the customer's diary. Never a scare, never felling as the answer.

cards.title: Something done to the tree once, and left
cards.brief: A tree topped years ago and now a mass of thin shoots on rotting stubs, a cut made flush to the trunk that never closed, a stump ground shallow so it keeps shooting, ivy pulled off and the bark torn with it, a stake left on until it cut into the trunk, a cable fitted and never looked at again (Table B done badly rows for this service). The one cause this card makes: an old cut or a half job the tree has grown round. Say what the job does differently, from the Table A stages and the Table E facts (a cut kept outside the collar so the tree can close it; a reduction specified by size, never a percentage; support fitted with an inspection arranged); never a dig at whoever did it. On a schedule led page: a pollard or a hedge left past its cycle, and what bringing it back in stages involves, with no promise it will thicken or recover.
cards.mechanism: an old cut or a half job the tree has grown round

cards.title: It's getting worse, not settling down
cards.brief: A supported branch moving more than it did, a fork that has opened wider, an ash crown thinner this summer than last, shoots coming back from a stump, a lean the customer is sure has grown (Table B signs for cabling, ash dieback, stumps and removal). The one cause this card makes: a defect outpacing what holds it. Say honestly when support, pruning or watching stops being enough and removal becomes the right answer, from the trade facts: a support is not a cure and deterioration can outrun it; a diseased tree is assessed for risk and kept where it is safe to keep (Table A and E). Never that the tree is safe, never that it is doomed. Not an old cut left behind: card 2 owns that.
cards.mechanism: a defect outpacing what holds it

cards.title: A report someone else has asked you for
cards.brief: The customer has been asked for something in writing: a lender wants a tree report before a mortgage, building plans show trees close to the works, a council has sent a notice about branches over the pavement, an insurer wants a cause investigated, a landlord or an agent needs the trees looked at on a cycle (Table B surveys; Table C highway notice, with 'usually' and never the Act's name). The one cause this card makes: a question about the tree that needs a written answer. Say what a report does and does not do, from Table A and E: its scope is what was asked for, a lender's report is not a development survey, and no report proves a tree caused subsidence on its own. On a page other than Tree surveys and reports, the card reads as the written record of what was done (the work documented after an emergency; a support's inspection arrangement), from the Table A stages. Never legal advice, never a standard's number.
cards.mechanism: a question about the tree that needs a written answer

faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to. No promise to put it right free. Never invent a guarantee or insurance.

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission for [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts rule rows for this service only, put as the thing that usually applies, with 'usually' or 'in most cases'. A tree with an order on it: the council's consent comes first, in most cases. A tree in a conservation area: the council is told ahead of the work, the number of weeks only as the rule row gives it. A dead tree or an immediate danger has a narrower route (notice, or the necessary work and the council told after). A garden tree usually needs no felling licence. A nest in use, a bat roost or a badger sett changes the timing or the method. A countryside hedge has its own notice and cutting season; a garden hedge does not. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it, and whether the business does the paperwork only from [CV: handles_planning]. Never a standard's number, an Act's or an order's name, a diameter or legal advice. Where the rows give no rule, say no permission is usually needed for this work at a home and leave it there.

problem_card.title: Work that waits for the tree's own calendar
problem_card.brief: What the time of year does to this job, from the trade facts timing row for this service. Say first what is normal for the season: a tree bare in winter, leaves down early in a dry August, birds in the hedge in spring. The one cause this card makes: sap, leaves and nests deciding the month. Then the reason in the tree: pruning of most species after the leaves have hardened, the sap bleeders in summer or midwinter so they do not weep; planting and moving while dormant so the roots are not asked to work; a deciduous hedge renovated in midwinter and an evergreen in mid spring; the crown's health judged in leaf; and in spring and summer a nest being built or used stops that part until it is empty, with no blanket ban on the season (Table C and E). What the business itself checks only from confirmed practices (nesting_bird_check). No dates, nothing about a busy time of year.

cards.title: More light, more room or a clearer line
cards.brief: The customer's situation: a garden in shade by the afternoon, branches at the gutters or over the roof, a hedge too wide for the path, a view or a lamp lost behind growth, scrub taking the end of the garden. What decides it: how the tree or hedge regrows after the cut, from the trade facts for this service (a reduction cut back to suitable side branches keeps the shape and regrows evenly; a lift takes the lower branches for clearance; some evergreens never refill a cut into old wood; a hedge comes back to a width in stages over more than one season; topping leaves a mass of shoots on rotting stubs and is never offered). What the work gives them: light on the lawn, clearance from the house, a hedge back to a size that can be kept, a path through the scrub, with the tree looking like itself next summer. Leads on the crown reduction, hedge reduction and clearance pages. Never a fault invented for it, never a percentage, never a lifestyle pitch.
cards.mechanism: how the tree or hedge regrows after the cut

cards.title: A stump, a hedge or scrub where you want to use the ground
cards.brief: The customer's situation: a stump where a lawn, a bed, a shed base or a drive is planned, an old hedge where a fence is going, brambles over the ground that building work needs. What decides it: what the ground is wanted for afterwards, from the trade facts for this service (Table A and E stumps: the finish and the depth agreed to the intended use, deeper for planting than for grass, with no measurement given; the chippings cleared or left, the hole backfilled; some species shoot again from live roots and the bigger roots rot in their own time; Table A hedge removal and clearance: cut in sections, stumps out only if specified, protected hedges and nests checked first, written as what usually applies). What the work gives them: ground they can level, plant or build on, and an honest picture of what stays underneath. Leads on Tree stump removal, Hedge reduction and removal and Site and vegetation clearance. Never a number of years, never a promise that nothing grows back.
cards.mechanism: what the ground is wanted for afterwards

cards.title: A new tree, or one you'd rather move than lose
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want a tree where there is none, a tree to replace one that came down, screening from the road, or a tree that stands where an extension is going and they would rather move it than fell it. What decides it: the roots taking hold in the new ground, from the trade facts for this service (Table A planting: the position prepared, the roots kept from drying, the tree set at the right level, firmed, staked or guarded only where it needs it, watered through its first seasons; Table A transplanting: the root ball prepared, lifted and moved without drying, replanted and watched; Table A and E timing: while the tree is dormant, from autumn to early spring, bare root stock only in those months). The choice between bare root, root balled and container grown from the materials cell, with the reason. What the work gives them: a tree planted so it establishes rather than sits, and what it will need from them in its first summers. Leads on Tree planting and Tree transplanting. Never a promise it will take.
cards.mechanism: the roots taking hold in the new ground

cards.title: Logs, chippings and what the work leaves behind
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they have a wood burner and want the timber, they want chip for the paths or the beds, they have a pile of brash from the last job, or they own a piece of woodland and want it looked after rather than left. What decides it: what the timber is worth to you where it stands, from the trade facts for this service (Table A chipping: chips left on site for a use or taken away; Table A firewood: cut, split and stacked under cover to dry, with the sale rules for logs only as the rule row gives them and never a moisture figure or a volume; Table A woodland: a plan, thinning or coppicing to it, licences and designations checked, written as what usually applies). What the work gives them: timber and chip that are useful rather than a heap, and a wood managed to a plan. Logs left for the customer, or sold, only from the client values. Leads on Wood chipping, Firewood and logs and Woodland management. Never a seasoning time in months.
cards.mechanism: what the timber is worth to you where it stands

problem_card.title: Getting the timing right for the tree
problem_card.brief: The customer's situation: they want the garden sorted before summer, or want to know when a tree should go in or come back. What decides it: the window the species gives, from the trade facts timing cell for this service (planting and moving while dormant, from autumn to early spring; a reduction once the leaves have hardened, the sap bleeders in summer or midwinter; a deciduous hedge renovated in midwinter and an evergreen one in mid spring; clearance and stump work when the ground carries the machines; a nest being built or used leaving that part until it is empty, with no blanket ban on the season). What the work gives them: a job done in its window so the tree or the hedge takes it well. No dates, nothing about spring or autumn being busy, no promise about the weather.

No dates, no number of hours or days, no promises about the weather. This is the one place the timing is written.

cost.h2: What Moves the Price of an Emergency Call Out in [CITY]

cards.title: When you call
cards.brief: The time of day and the day of the week move the price: an evening, a night or a weekend against a weekday morning, and a crew called out from home against one already on the road (Table F emergency tree work: out of hours mobilisation). A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; never say there is no charge for coming out unless [CV: quote_call_out_fee] says there is none. Whether the business comes out at those hours only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; when it is not set, nothing about hours at all. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting to you
cards.brief: How far the tree is from the base and what is between the van and the tree: a tree across a road with traffic to keep back, a limb on a neighbour's roof, a back garden with no way in for a chipper or a platform, a lane too narrow for the lorry (Table F emergency tree work: roads or live lines, restricted access). Distance and access move the price; say why in plain words. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; never hours of cover unless [CV: out_of_hours_available] says so.

cards.title: Making it safe first
cards.brief: What is done first on a call out, from Table A emergency tree work: the danger judged from the ground, the area closed off, lines and anything the tree could still fall on checked, then only the hung up limb or the split stem brought down or lowered under control. How long that takes and how many people it needs is what the first part of the price pays for: a limb caught over a path is one thing, a tree on a roof with the timber still loaded is another (Table F: unstable or suspended wood). Never how it is done beyond this; never a promise that it is all finished on the day.

cards.title: What's on the van and what has to come later
cards.brief: The saws, the ropes and a chipper come with the crew; a platform, a crane or a bigger chipper has to be booked and brought, and a line waits for the network operator (Table A emergency tree work: a platform or mechanical methods according to the tree; Table F: specialist equipment). What is left once the danger is dealt with, the rest of the tree, the stump and the timber, is a second visit priced as its own job (Table A: follow up work may be separate). Say what decides it and give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cards.title: A tree on the house, the shed or the car
cards.brief: A tree or a big limb that has come down onto the roof, through a fence, across a car or a conservatory, or into next door's garden (Table B emergency and removal: a misjudged fall or a failed tree onto an occupied area). The one cause this card makes: the weight of the tree still on what it fell on, which can shift as the structure under it gives or as the wind moves the crown. Write the reader's situation, why it won't keep, and what usually happens when they call: the danger judged from the ground, the area and the rooms beneath kept clear, the weight taken off in pieces under control from the top down, the building left for whoever repairs it (Table A emergency: remove only the immediate hazard, make the site safe). Never a response time or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it; whether the business deals with the insurer only from the client values.
cards.mechanism: the weight of the tree still on what it fell on

cards.title: A storm damaged tree that's still standing
cards.brief: A trunk split down the middle, a tree leaning since last night, large branches torn out and the rest of the crown lopsided, soil lifted on one side of the base (Table B removal signs). The one cause this card makes: a split or a new lean the wind has not finished with, because a tree that has part failed carries the rest on wood that has already given once. What the customer does first: keep clear of the side it leans to and of anything under it, never try to rope or prop it. What usually happens: the tree looked at from the ground, the immediate danger taken down in sections, and the decision about what is left made once it can be seen properly (Table A removal: dismantle in sections where the fall zone is not clear). Never that the tree will be fine, never that it must all come down before it has been looked at.
cards.mechanism: a split or a new lean the wind has not finished with

cards.title: Made safe today, the rest planned properly
cards.brief: The reader wants to know what an emergency visit does and does not do. The one cause this card makes: only the immediate danger removed on the day, because working under unstable timber and in a storm is where people get hurt, and the stump, the timber and the rest of the tree are safer and cheaper done as planned work (Table A emergency: remove only the immediate hazard, make safe, document; follow up work may be separate; Table F: the price falls where the hazard can be isolated by limited safe making work). Say what usually happens on the day (the area closed off, lines and protections checked, the hanging or fallen wood brought down under control, the way cleared) and what comes back as a quote for another day. Never promise everything is finished on the first visit; never a price.
cards.mechanism: only the immediate danger removed on the day

cards.title: A protected tree that's become dangerous
cards.brief: The customer knows or suspects the tree has an order on it or stands in a conservation area, and it is now hanging over the road or split to the ground. The one cause this card makes: the council told after the danger is dealt with, not before, which is the narrow route that usually applies where there is an immediate risk of serious harm: only the work needed to remove the danger is done, and the council is told in writing as soon as practicable; a dead tree with no immediate danger usually has notice given first instead; a duty to plant a replacement can follow (Table C, written as what usually applies, never the Act's or the order's name). Say what the business records and sends only from the Table A documenting stage and [CV: handles_planning]. Never advice to the customer to skip the council because it is urgent, and never that inconvenience or worry counts as danger.
cards.mechanism: the council told after the danger is dealt with, not before

steps.title: Call Us
steps.brief: What to say: what has happened, where the tree or the branch is (across the road or the drive, on a roof or a car, caught up in the crown, touching or near an overhead line), whether anyone is hurt, whether anything is still hanging. What to do meanwhile, in plain words: keep people, cars and pets away from it and from anything it could still fall on; never try to cut it, drag it or prop it; anything touching a line is left alone and the electricity network operator is called. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Make the Area Safe
steps.brief: On arrival the danger is judged from the ground first, the area closed off, lines and protections checked, then only the immediate hazard is brought down or lowered under control (Table A emergency tree work). The price for making it safe agreed before anyone comes out only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]; what the rest costs waits until the tree has been seen. Never restates 'free'. 'Same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes.

steps.title: We Clear the Danger and Plan the Rest
steps.brief: What usually happens: the hazard removed, the area left safe, the work written up and any notice the council needs sent (Table A: document the work and the required notices; Table C: a protected tree made safe because it was an immediate danger has only the necessary work done and the council told as soon as practicable, written as what usually applies). What is left of the tree, the stump and the timber is dealt with as planned work on another day (Table A: follow up work may be separate). Never promise everything is done on the first visit. Never mention the price.

faq_slots.question: How much is an emergency [TRADE_PERSON] call out in [CITY]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What moves the price, from the cost cards: the time of day and the day of the week, how far the tree is from the base, the access, what making it safe takes, and that the rest of the tree, the stump and the timber are a second visit priced as its own job. A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; the hours the business comes out only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; an arrival time only from [CV: response_time]. The price agreed before work starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice. No figure.

faq_slots.question: How quickly can you get here?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only, as given; a same day visit only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes; work in the tree waits until the wind has dropped and the timber can be reached safely, and a line is dealt with by the network operator first (Table A emergency). Never '24/7' or 'any time' unless [CV: emergency_callouts] gives it in those words. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Will you come out while the storm is still going?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What usually happens: the area made safe and the danger judged from the ground as soon as it is safe to be there; while the wind is still up nobody climbs or works under hung up timber, and a live line waits for the network operator (Table A emergency). Any arrival time from [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only; no out of hours promise unless [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: response_time] gives it. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for emergency [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with a plausible tree work example that does not suggest carelessness. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after an emergency job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then that making safe is making safe: the planned work that follows is where the tree, the stump and the timber are dealt with properly, under the reasonable care and skill standard, never as a defence. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What should I do before you arrive?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From a safe distance only: keep people, cars and pets clear of the tree and of anything it could still fall on, stay out of rooms under a tree on the roof, touch nothing in contact with an overhead line and call the network operator about the line first, photograph what can be seen from the ground (Table B and C emergency). Never an instruction to cut, pull, prop or climb. Whether the business deals with the insurer only from the client values.

faq_slots.question: Is this an emergency, or can it wait?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What counts as urgent for this service, from the card list and the trade facts signs row: a tree or a limb down across a road, a drive, a roof or a car; a torn branch still hanging over where people go; anything touching or near an overhead line; a trunk split or a tree leaning freshly after a storm. What usually waits for planned work, from the Table B rows: a stump, a tree that has simply grown too big, a hedge over the path, dead wood high in a crown over a bed nobody uses, a lean the tree has had for years. Link the planned sibling page or the category page. Planned work is never dressed up as urgent.

problem_card.title: A protected tree that's become dangerous
problem_card.brief: The customer knows or suspects the tree has an order on it or stands in a conservation area, and it is now hanging over the road or split to the ground. The one cause this card makes: the council told after the danger is dealt with, not before, which is the narrow route that usually applies where there is an immediate risk of serious harm: only the work needed to remove the danger is done, and the council is told in writing as soon as practicable; a dead tree with no immediate danger usually has notice given first instead; a duty to plant a replacement can follow (Table C, written as what usually applies, never the Act's or the order's name). Say what the business records and sends only from the Table A documenting stage and [CV: handles_planning]. Never advice to the customer to skip the council because it is urgent, and never that inconvenience or worry counts as danger.
problem_card.mechanism: the council told after the danger is dealt with, not before

cards.title: Trees older than the houses around them
cards.brief: Big mature trees in the older streets: a crown over three gardens, roots under a shared wall, branches at the bedroom windows of a house that was built close to a tree already there. The one cause this card makes: mature trees left from before the street was built, which the town profile dates (villas with their original planting, a street tree line, a park edge). Tie the age to what the work involves, never to a judgement on the trees' state: a tree of that size comes down in sections lowered by rope rather than felled, pruning is specified by size back to growth points, and in the older parts of a town an order or a conservation area usually covers the tree, so the council has a say first ('usually', never the order's or the area's official name; from the dossier rules only). Never that the town's old trees are dangerous or neglected.
cards.mechanism: mature trees left from before the street was built

cards.title: Streets where the council has a say first
cards.brief: An owner who wants a tree reduced or taken down and is told it cannot simply be booked. The one cause this card makes: a notice or a consent before the first cut, where the town profile and the dossier rules give conservation areas or protected trees. What usually applies, in plain words and without an Act's or an order's name. A tree with an order on it: the council's consent comes first, in most cases. A tree in a conservation area: the council is told ahead of the work, the number of weeks only as the trade facts rule row gives it, and only where the dossier says the street is covered. A dead tree or an immediate danger has a narrower route of its own. Which council handles it only from the dossier. Whether the business sends the notice or makes the application for the customer only from [CV: handles_planning]. Never claim a street or an estate is covered without the research.
cards.mechanism: a notice or a consent before the first cut

cards.title: Ground that moves with the trees
cards.brief: Cracks a house near a big tree shows at the end of a dry summer, a tree blown over in the first autumn gale, paths lifted by roots that stay near the surface. The one cause this card makes: the town's soil shrinking, or staying shallow, under its trees; the town profile and a symptom say which (clay that gives up its moisture to a big tree through a dry summer and takes it back in winter, so the ground under a house rises and falls; thin soil over chalk or rock where roots stay shallow and a tree catches the wind; an exposed hill or coast). Say what it means for the work in plain words: on clay a worry about a house is investigated before anything is cut, because felling can bring movement of its own (Table E subsidence), and a reduction, or a barrier that steers the roots, is often the better answer; on shallow ground a leaning tree after a gale is looked at from the ground first. Never diagnose any house, never promise the ground will settle.
cards.mechanism: the town's soil shrinking, or staying shallow, under its trees

cards.title: Young trees planted close to new houses
cards.brief: A tree put in by the builder a stride from the wall, now at the gutters; a row of the same species along a new estate's road; a small garden with a tree that will be twice the house's height. The one cause this card makes: trees planted small against a house they have now reached, where the town profile gives the newer estates. What it means for the work, never a judgement on the planting: a reduction specified by size to keep the clearance, repeated as the tree grows, or an honest conversation about replacing it with a tree that fits the space (Table A pruning and planting); on clay, the distance to the house is part of that conversation (Table E). Ash dieback on an estate's ash only where the research confirms it locally. Never name a species the profile does not give.
cards.mechanism: trees planted small against a house they have now reached

faq_slots.question: When is the best time of year for [WORK_LOWER] work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: When each kind of tree work is best done and why, in the tree or in what usually applies, from the trade facts timing cells: felling, dismantling and stump work through the year when the ground and the weather allow; pruning generally after the leaves have hardened, the sap bleeders in summer or midwinter; planting and moving while dormant; a nest being built or used leaving that part until it is empty, with no blanket ban on the season. cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How much you order
cards.brief: A bag, a bulk bag or a loose load: the quantity moves the price more than anything else, and timber that still has to be cut to length and split costs more than logs already processed (Table F firewood and logs: cross cutting and splitting required, handling and storage). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Seasoned or kiln dried against green
cards.brief: Green timber straight from a job against logs that have been stacked under cover and dried, or kiln dried: the drying, the storage and the moisture check are time and space the price has to carry (Table A: season or otherwise dry, check moisture; Table F: drying and moisture checking, certification where required). A load sold as certified only where the client values say the business holds the certification; never a time in the stack as proof the logs are dry (Table E: elapsed time is not certification). No figure.

cards.title: Hardwood against softwood
cards.brief: What the logs are: hardwood against softwood, a mixed load from the week's work against a load of one kind picked out for the customer (Table A: select suitable timber). Say that what the customer burns and what they burn it in decides it, in their words; never a species list as a promise of what is in stock.

cards.title: Delivery and stacking
cards.brief: How far the logs travel from the yard, whether the van can tip at the door or the bags are carried through to the store, and whether the logs are left in the bag or stacked where they will keep dry (Table F: delivery handling; Table A: stack with ventilation and weather protection). Collection from the yard only where the client values say it is offered. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us What You Burn and How Much You Need
steps.brief: What to say: the stove or the open fire they burn in, whether they want seasoned, kiln dried or green logs to dry themselves, how much (a bag, a bulk bag, a load) and where it goes when it arrives. The number from [CV: phone], the form only from [CV: quote_method]. Nothing about what is in stock here.

steps.title: We Confirm What's in Stock and the Price
steps.brief: What usually happens: the business says what it has (timber from its own work, cut and split, seasoned or green), whether the quantity asked for is there, and the price for the load and the delivery, from [CV: quote_method] and [CV: price_list] only. Dryness said as what has been done to the logs and the moisture check (Table A), never as a time in the stack (Table E). Never restates 'free'.

steps.title: We Deliver on a Day That Suits You
steps.brief: The delivery: the load tipped or the bags carried to where it was agreed, stacked only where that was part of the price. Said without a day or a window unless [CV: start_time] gives one. Never mention the price.

cards.title: How much brash there is
cards.brief: The volume and the bulk of what goes through the chipper: a heap of hedge trimmings against the crown of a felled tree, brash already dragged to one place against branches left where they fell (Table F wood chipping: volume and bulk of brash, distance from the chipper). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting the chipper to it
cards.brief: Where the chipper can stand and how far the brash has to be carried to it: a drive beside the heap against a back garden reached through a side gate too narrow for the machine, nowhere for the lorry to park, a lane that has to be kept clear (Table F: restricted vehicle access; Table A: set the chipper and the exclusion area). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: Whether the chip stays or goes
cards.brief: Chip blown into a corner of the garden for the beds and the paths against chip loaded and taken away: taking it costs the transport and the destination (Table F: off site transport and destination; Table E: chip from ordinary tree work may be left on site under the agency's conditions, said as what usually applies and never as an exemption's name). Whether the business takes it away only from the confirmed practices and [CV: waste_carrier_registered].

cards.title: The time on site
cards.brief: How long the crew and the machine are there, which the three cards above set between them: clean brash fed steadily goes quickly, brash tangled with wire, soil or stone has to be sorted first (Table A: segregate suitable brash; Table F: suitable clean feedstock). Say what decides it and give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many trees and how big the site is
cards.brief: One tree in a garden against a line of trees on a boundary or every tree on a development plot: the number of trees and the ground to cover move the price first (Table F tree surveys and reports: number of trees, site complexity). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: What kind of report you've been asked for
cards.brief: A report for a mortgage lender, a survey for a planning application, or a decay or subsidence investigation: each has its own scope and its own method, and a lender's report has the scope the lender asks for, not the planning survey's (Table A: agree the report purpose, apply the relevant assessment method; Table E: a mortgage tree report is not automatically the development survey). Say that the customer tells us who wants it and why, and the report is scoped to that. Never a standard's number.

cards.title: From the ground or from the tree
cards.brief: A visual inspection from the ground against a climbing inspection or decay testing where a defect high up or inside the stem has to be looked at closely (Table A: inspect and measure the trees, apply the relevant method; Table F: specialist decay or subsidence investigation). Say why a closer look costs more time and more kit, in plain words.

cards.title: One visit or a cycle
cards.brief: A single report against an estate, a school or a business that wants its trees looked at again on a cycle, with the plans and the records from last time reused (Table F: repeat visits; existing usable plans and records lower the price). No interval given as a rule: the pack says the revisit interval varies, and the duty is proportionate care, not a universal inspection interval (Table A; Table C occupiers' liability). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How long and how deep the trench is
cards.brief: The length of the line the barrier has to run and the depth it has to go to, which the product and the roots set, not a rule of thumb (Table F root barriers: trench length, product specific depth; Table A: depth and position are product and site specific). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: What has to come up and go back
cards.brief: A trench in open ground against one through a patio, a path or a drive that has to be lifted and relaid behind it (Table F: hard surface removal and reinstatement). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: What's crossing the line
cards.brief: Pipes, cables and drains in the way of the trench, found before anything is dug, and roots that have to be worked round rather than cut through so the tree is not harmed (Table A: locate buried services, excavate while managing root impacts; Table F: buried services, root sensitive excavation). Say why a crowded trench is slower work.

cards.title: The barrier itself
cards.brief: A plain barrier against a ribbed one that steers the roots, and the length and depth of it: the product only from [CV: materials_methods], never a brand or a make the client values do not give (Table A: a linear root barrier or a ribbed root directing system). Say what decides it and give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.
